q: What problem does the Viterbi algorithm solve?
short: It finds the single most probable hidden state sequence for an observation sequence in an HMM (decoding), exactly and efficiently with dynamic programming.
follow: Which other HMM problems are there?

q: Write the Viterbi recurrence.
short: v₁(j) = πⱼbⱼ(o₁); vₜ(j) = maxᵢ vₜ₋₁(i)·aᵢⱼ·bⱼ(oₜ); backpointer btₜ(j) = argmaxᵢ vₜ₋₁(i)aᵢⱼ; end with maxⱼ v_T(j) and backtrace.

q: Why do we need backpointers?
short: The table stores only scores; to recover the actual best sequence we need to know which predecessor achieved each max, then follow those pointers back from the best final cell.
mistakes: Taking the best cell per column independently.

q: Viterbi vs forward algorithm?
short: Same lattice; Viterbi takes the max over predecessors (best path), forward takes the sum (total probability of the observations over all paths).
detail: Forward–backward uses both directions for training.

q: What is Viterbi's time complexity and why?
short: O(N²T): N·T cells, each a max over N predecessors. Space O(NT) for scores and backpointers.
follow: How does beam search change it?

q: What is a MEMM?
short: A discriminative sequence model that applies multinomial logistic regression at each position: P(tᵢ | wᵢ, tᵢ₋₁, other features) = softmax(θ·f); decoded with Viterbi.

q: Greedy vs Viterbi decoding for a MEMM?
short: Greedy commits to the best tag at each word given the previous chosen tag, fast but can't recover from early errors; Viterbi maximises the product over the whole sentence.

q: List limitations of HMM taggers.
short: Zero emissions for unknown words, inability to use rich overlapping features, limited (one-tag) context and output independence, sparsity of counts, and left-to-right-only modelling.

q: Fill the 'is' column for 'the doctor is in'.
Run Viterbi on the weather HMM for observations 3, 1.
follow: Add a day with 3 ice creams?

q: Compute the MEMM softmax for scores VB 2.0, NN 0.5.
Explain the label-bias problem.
short: In a locally normalised model each state's outgoing probabilities sum to 1 regardless of the observation, so states with few successors pass on their mass almost unconditionally; paths through them can't be penalised by bad evidence. CRFs normalise over whole sequences, removing it.

q: Why work in log space for Viterbi?
short: Products of many probabilities underflow; using sums of log probabilities is stable, and max is preserved by the monotone log.
follow: Does log space work for forward?
mistakes: Using log-sum-exp for Viterbi (needed only for forward).

q: How does beam search relate to Viterbi?
short: Beam search keeps only the top-k scoring states (or partial sequences) per step, trading exactness for speed when N is large or the model isn't Markov (e.g. neural decoders).

q: HMM vs MEMM?
short: HMM: generative, models P(w | t)P(t), trained by counting, can't use overlapping features. MEMM: discriminative, models P(t | w, t₋₁) with arbitrary features via logistic regression, trained by gradient descent, but suffers label bias. Both use Viterbi.
mistakes: Saying MEMMs don't need tagged data.

q: Design features for an MEMM POS tagger.
short: Current word identity and lowercased form; prefixes/suffixes up to 4 characters; capitalisation, digits, hyphens; word shape (Xxxx, dd-dd); previous and next words; previous tag and tag bigram; combinations like prev tag + current suffix. Regularise weights and prune rare features.
detail: Unknown words handled by shape and affixes.
mistakes: Using future tags as features (not available).

q: Prove Viterbi's optimal-substructure property.
short: If the best path to (j, t) passes through (i, t−1), its prefix must be the best path to (i, t−1); otherwise swapping in a better prefix would give a better path to (j, t) because later factors aᵢⱼbⱼ(oₜ) don't depend on the prefix (Markov property).
detail: This justifies keeping one path per cell.
mistakes: Applying Viterbi to models with long-range dependencies.

q: How does a CRF differ from a MEMM in training and inference?
short: A linear-chain CRF scores the whole sequence, P(t | w) = exp(Σᵢ θ·f(tᵢ₋₁, tᵢ, w, i))/Z(w), with one global normaliser Z computed by the forward algorithm; gradients need forward–backward marginals. Inference still uses Viterbi. No label bias.
mistakes: Thinking CRFs need a different decoder.

q: When might greedy decoding be good enough?
short: When local decisions are reliable and rarely depend on later context (strong features, bidirectional encoders that already see the whole sentence), or when latency matters; measure the accuracy gap on validation data.
detail: Neural taggers often decode greedily with small loss.
mistakes: Assuming greedy is always much worse.

q: You need to tag 1 billion words per day. How do you make Viterbi fast?
short: Use a reduced tagset or tag dictionary (only allowed tags per word, shrinking N), beam pruning, log-space integer arithmetic, vectorised lattice operations, batching, caching frequent sentences, and parallelise across documents.
